study.title: 1 Peter 2 - Grow into the Word, live as God's people, and follow the example of Christ
study.overview: In this chapter, Peter unites identity and practice. He calls believers to abandon attitudes that destroy fellowship and to intensely desire the Word of God, because it is through it that the new birth matures. Then he presents Christ as the living and principal stone, rejected by some precious to those who believe; in union with him, the church is formed as a spiritual house, holy priesthood and people acquired to proclaim the virtues of God. He then applies this identity to public and social life: holiness among the Gentiles, submission to the authorities, honor to all, fear of God and correct attitude even in unjust labor relations. The chapter culminates in Christ as a model of innocent suffering: he did not sin, did not return offense, trusted in the just Judge, took our sins and now leads the people who walked aviated back to the care of the Shepherd and Supervisor of souls.

outline.title: Leave the sin and desire the Word
outline.explanation: Peter orders them to set aside malice, deception, pretending, envy and maledicence. In contrast, believers must desire pure spiritual food as newborns desire milk, to grow through it, having already proved the goodness of the Lord.

outline.title: Christ, living stone, and the human answer
outline.explanation: Jesus is presented as the living stone, rejected by men but chosen by God. Believers are built with him as living stones, forming a spiritual house and a holy priesthood. The Scriptures already announced the main cornerstone; for those who believe, it is precious, but for the rebels it is a stumbling block, and its fall is linked to the rejection of the word.

outline.title: Identity of God's people and full public life
outline.explanation: Believers receive titles applied to the people of God: chosen generation, royal priesthood, holy nation and acquired people, in order to proclaim the virtues of God. As pilgrims, they must flee from the fleshly passions and maintain good conduct among the Gentiles. Peter then guides submission to the human authorities, the correct use of Christian freedom, universal honor, brotherly love, fear of God and honor to the king.

outline.title: Unjust suffering and the example of Christ
outline.explanation: Servants must submit to you not only kind, but also severe, when they suffer for conscience before God. Suffering for the good practiced is pleasing to God because Christ also suffered, leaving example: without sin, without deceit, without retaliation, delivered to the just Judge. He took away sins in their own body on the tree, so that believers die for sin and live for righteousness; now, healed by their wounds, they return to the Shepherd and Supervisor of their souls.

study.context: The notes highlight that Peter continues the exhortation initiated in the previous chapter, linking this teaching to the new birth and the incorruptible Word. They also note that, in the original world of the recipients, there were suspicions against Christians as possible disturbers of public order, which helps to understand why Peter deals with the submission to the authorities and the good testimony among the Gentiles. The allusions of the chapter to passages of Isaiah and Psalm 34 show that Peter reads the Christian experience in the light of the Scriptures of Israel.
study.theology: The chapter brings together sanctification, ecclesiology, Christology and public ethics. Holiness is not presented as mere moral effort, but as a response to the new birth and food of the Word. The church is defined in union with Christ: it is the main stone, foundation, and criterion of division between faith and rebellion. The titles of 9 to 10 indicate that the people of God are constituted for proclaiming, mission, and mercy received, not on their own merit. Christian ethics includes civil submission, social respect and patience in unjust suffering, because freedom in Christ is not a license to malice. At the center is the substitute and exemplary work of Jesus: he suffers without sin, carries sins of others, heals and brings the flock back to the pastoral care of God. The reference to be 'targeted' on verse 8 should be treated with caution, because the notes show a divergent reading about whether this points to divine decree or to the consequence of unbelief.

scholarViews.insight: The expression of those who stumble in the word for being rebellious is difficult, and the note notes that it is not clear whether they were destined by God's initiative to unbelief or, because of their own unbelief, to condemnation.
The call to abandon malice and other evils is presented as necessary because such sins destroy charity and prevent the effectiveness of the word, hindering regeneration itself.
The expressions 'chosen generation' and 'real priesthood' apply to Christians titles before given to the people of Israel, indicating a people gathered in Christ, whether of Jewish origin or Gentile.

questions: What attitudes Peter commands to abandon first, and why do they harm spiritual growth?
What does it mean, in practice, to be 'living stones' and form a 'spiritual house' in Christ?
How does the example of Christ in his sufferings correct the way I react to injustices and offenses?
study.practice: Examine your speech, your desires and your reactions: is there malice, pretending, envy, or evil words to abandon? Set up regular time to desire the Word with the same urgency as a baby by milk, not only to learn more, but to grow in holiness. In daily life, practice good public conduct, respect for authorities and honor people, without using Christian freedom as an excuse for sin. If you suffer unjustly, choose to answer without retaliation, trusting in God and remembering that Christ suffered before you and for you.
study.uncertainty: Notes do not provide additional historical details about date, exact location or specific conditions of the letter, so these points should not be magnified beyond what the text and comments allow. There is also an interpretative tension on verse 8 on the meaning of 'targeted', and the study cannot treat it as resolved in an absolute way. In addition, the images of 'spiritual sacrifices' and 'real priesthood' are explained from the notes, but without imposing a single denominational tradition.
